content: A mirror image is essentially a duplicate of an object or image, created through reflection in a mirror. In two-dimensional geometry, the mirror image of an object is a virtual image formed by reflection in a plane mirror. This image is identical in size to the original object but differs in orientation unless the object exhibits reflection symmetry, also known as P-symmetry. For example, if a point on an object has coordinates (x, y, z), its mirror image, reflected across the y-z plane, will have coordinates (-x, y, z). This demonstrates that mirror reflection involves a reversal of the coordinate axis perpendicular to the mirror's surface. Consequently, a mirror image does not reverse left and right or up and down but instead reverses front and back. Two-dimensional mirror images can be observed in the reflections of mirrors or other reflective surfaces, as well as in printed text viewed from the reverse side. The concept of a mirror image extends to three-dimensional objects, including their internal structures, even if they are not transparent. In this context, the term mirror image encompasses both structural and visual aspects and is also referred to as an enantiomer or enantiomorph. A three-dimensional mirror image appears to change as the observer moves, due to the shifting relative positions of objects from the observer's perspective. Observing a mirror from different positions, while remaining within the half-space on one side of the mirror, is akin to viewing the three-dimensional mirror image of the space. Without additional mirrors, only the mirror image of the half-space in front of the mirror is relevant. However, if another mirror is present, the mirror image of the other half-space becomes visible as well. Mirror images are sometimes deliberately used in text to make it readable through a mirror. For instance, emergency vehicles like ambulances and fire engines often display their names in mirror image so that drivers can read them correctly in their rear-view mirrors. Additionally, some movie theaters employ a Rear Window Captioning System to assist individuals with hearing impairments in following the film. When two mirrors are positioned at an angle (α) to each other, viewing through both mirrors from the sector formed by the intersection of their half-spaces creates an effect similar to observing a version of the world rotated by an angle of 2α. The points of observation and viewing directions correspond to those seen through a frame defined by the first mirror and its mirror image with respect to the second mirror. If the mirrors have vertical edges, the left edge of the field of view corresponds to the plane formed by the right edge of the first mirror and the edge of the second mirror. This edge appears on the right when viewed directly but on the left in the mirror image. In the case of two parallel mirrors, looking through both mirrors once creates the effect of viewing a version of the world translated by twice the distance between the mirrors, in a direction perpendicular to them and away from the observer. Since the plane of the mirror being directly observed lies beyond that of the other mirror, the observer always views the scene at an oblique angle. The translation effect includes a component away from the observer and another in a perpendicular direction. This translated view can also be described as a translation of the observer in the opposite direction. For example, with a vertical periscope, the world appears shifted away from the observer and downward by the length of the periscope. However, it is often more practical to consider the equivalent shift of the observer, which would be upward and backward.
